FULL PIPELINE EXECUTED (script: /workspace/analysis_nls_bmi_tp.py; outputs: analysis_results.csv, analysis_summary.txt). All models as approved: weights converted lb→kg, 1985 height (inches) as the common BMI denominator, BMI winsorized 1–99%, TP ordinal score (PUT IN=0, NO CHANGE=1, TOOK OUT=2, NO SAVINGS=3), covariates = age-1981, sex, race (2 dummies), log family income (1985, 1979 fallback), log family wealth 1985, grade 1979, ASVAB composite, and — per your note — an incarceration dummy (residence=Jail in any of 1985–1989; 300 respondents, clean code 5, included in the primary model; its own coefficient −0.981, 95% CI [−1.477, −0.485]).

KEY RESULTS (OLS, HC1 robust SEs; n in parentheses)
Primary — BMI_1989 (n=10,167):
- Per +1 present-bias point: +0.143 [0.063, 0.223]
- High TP {took out, no savings} vs {put in, no change}: +0.290 [0.107, 0.472]
- 4-dummy vs PUT IN: TOOK OUT +0.435 [0.206, 0.664]; NO CHANGE +0.377 [0.104, 0.649]; NO SAVINGS +0.425 [0.170, 0.681]
Raw vs adjusted: unadjusted slope +0.285 [0.208, 0.361]; raw mean gap PUT IN vs NO SAVINGS = +0.89 BMI (24.50 vs 25.39); adjusted gap ≈ +0.43 (adjusted means 24.78 vs 25.21) — covariates (age, sex, race, income, wealth, education, ability, incarceration) absorb roughly half the raw association.
Secondary outcomes:
- BMI_1992 (n=8,322): +0.186 [0.088, 0.285] — association persists 3 years after the savings window.
- ΔBMI 1981→1989 + baseline BMI (n=9,927): +0.031 [−0.024, +0.086] (score); +0.082 [−0.042, +0.206] (high TP) — NOT significant. Per your note, stated explicitly: because every BMI uses the 1985 height denominator, this "change" model is effectively a weight-change model expressed in BMI units; it does not capture adult height change. The TP–BMI association is a LEVEL difference (high-TP respondents were already heavier in 1981: 22.80 vs 22.27), not a differential weight-gain effect.
Robustness battery:
- Drop NO SAVINGS (n=7,123): +0.215 [0.100, 0.329] — still positive (larger).
- Sex-stratified: males +0.024 [−0.076, +0.124] n.s.; females +0.250 [0.127, 0.374] — association concentrated in women.
- Winsorization: 1–99% +0.143 (primary); trim [12,45] +0.146; no winsorization +0.068 [−0.054, +0.191] n.s. (unadjusted no-winsorization still +0.238). 54 implausible BMI>45 values (up to 176) mostly in high-TP groups; the adjusted estimate is sensitive to them, so the winsorized specification is the defensible primary.
- Ordered logit on obesity category (normal/overweight/obese): OR=1.019 per TP point [0.984, 1.056] n.s. — the association is on the continuous BMI level, small relative to the 25/30 category thresholds.
- Listwise deletion of covariates (no imputation, n=8,274): +0.170 [0.081, 0.258] — consistent.
- Continuous net saving flow (log$, put-in vs took-out subsample, n=5,614): −0.029 [−0.045, −0.013] per log $ — more net saving → lower BMI, same direction as the categorical measure.

DATA-GROUNDED HYPOTHESIS (answer to "Does increased time preference lead to higher BMI?"):
In NLSY79 respondents, higher time preference — operationalized as present-biased savings behaviour over 1985–1989 (taking money out of or having no savings, versus putting money in) — is associated with higher BMI. Each one-point step up the four-level present-bias scale is associated with ~0.14 BMI units higher in 1989 (95% CI 0.06–0.22) and ~0.19 units higher in 1992 (0.09–0.29), after adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, family income, wealth, education, cognitive ability and incarceration; non-savers differ from savers by ~0.43 adjusted BMI units (raw gap ~0.9, about half explained by demographics/finances). The association is a level difference, concentrated in women, that persists three years after the savings window, so the direction of the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that increased time preference leads to higher BMI; however, the design is observational (single 1985–89 savings snapshot, R/spouse household measure, 16.7% missingness correlated with sex and weight, reverse causality from health to savings not excluded) and the data establish a positive association, not causation.

LIMITATIONS: (1) time preference is a proxy from one savings-flow question, not a discount-rate measure; (2) NO SAVINGS conflates present bias with lack of savings access (dropping it strengthens, not weakens, the result); (3) estimate sensitive to implausible extreme BMI values (primary uses 1–99% winsorization); (4) ΔBMI null means no evidence of accelerated gain; (5) unit corrections (weights=lb, 1985 height=in; 1981 height excluded) are evidence-based inferences, not documentation.

payload.hypothesis: In NLSY79, higher time preference (present-biased savings flow 1985-89: took out or no savings vs put in) is associated with higher BMI: +0.143 BMI per present-bias point in 1989 (95% CI 0.063-0.223, n=10,167) and +0.186 in 1992 (0.088-0.285, n=8,322), adjusting for age, sex, race, income, wealth, education, ASVAB and incarceration; the raw saver vs non-saver gap (~0.9 BMI) is halved (~0.43) after adjustment. The association is a level difference (concentrated in women), not a differential 1981-1989 weight-gain effect (delta model n.s.), and persists 3 years after the savings window - directionally consistent with increased time preference leading to higher BMI, though the observational design supports association rather than proven causation.
payload.workflow: Inspected data (units: weights=lb, 1985 height=in, 1981 height excluded); built BMI_1981/1989/1992 from 1985 height, winsorized 1-99%; coded TP ordinal score from 1989 savings categorical; fitted OLS (HC1) primary (BMI_1989 ~ TP score, TP high, 4-dummy), secondary (BMI_1992, delta BMI + baseline), robustness (drop NO SAVINGS, sex-stratified, winsorization sensitivity, ordered logit on obesity category, listwise deletion, continuous net saving flow); compared raw vs adjusted magnitudes; added 1985-89 incarceration dummy to primary model.
